_note: uv sync --extra crafter (crafter-gym, gym/crafter/, pulls crafter), then pip install --force-reinstall 'crafter @ git+https://github.com/chengfanbrain/crafter.git@deterministic' -- a fork of 1.8.3 whose single change is that a seed plus an action list replays exactly (see _state_note). Plain PyPI crafter runs this config fine and plays identically to a subject, but its blocks cannot be replayed, so a model cannot be given the same episode. This is the paradigm's level 4 (survival): hostiles on, health/food/drink/energy decay, death ends the episode, nothing hidden from the HUD. It is stock crafter, rule for rule: what is written down below is the interface it is played through and the pacing, not the game. Levels 1-3 freeze or remove parts of the game and belong in a gymnasium.Wrapper shipped with the env, as the menu is (gym/crafter/crafter_gym/menu.py): a level an adapter applied would stop humans and models from playing the same game.
_why_one_config: There is one crafter config and it is this one, because the scanner has a button box and not a keyboard: the eight buttons here are the ones the rig's own frontend uses (crafter-for-brain-scan v0.33, core.py:ButtonMapper, frontend_pygame.py:KEYMAP), so a subject who practised in the rig keeps their fingers. A seventeen-key config existed until it was clear nobody would ever run it in a scanner; the env it used (Crafter-v0, no menu) is still registered and still what agents/ can be pointed at, and CrafterMenu-v0 is that same env under gym/crafter/crafter_gym/menu.py.
_menu_note: The wrapper's action space is Discrete(19): crafter's own 17, then cycle (17) and confirm (18). Y advances the cursor and steps the env with noop, X performs the action the cursor is on; both draw the cursor over the player for that one frame. The cost of a look is a turn, as it is in the rig: a free cycle would make all ten menu actions reachable for one press. The npz records the button in 'actions' and the engine's action in 'env_action', plus 'menu_idx' and 'menu_sel' read after the press, and action_names covers all 19 so the button column decodes. Two deviations from the rig, both deliberate: the cursor shows while the last press was cycle or confirm rather than for 3 wall-clock seconds (--menu-s), because a turn-based block repaints only on a press and has no clock to fade against, and this version is reconstructible from the logged actions alone; and the cursor sits at 3.5/9 of the frame height, the centre of the played area above crafter's own two HUD rows, which is where the rig puts it too.
_keys_note: Crafter's Discrete(17) map is 0=noop, 1=move_left, 2=move_right, 3=move_up, 4=move_down, 5=do, 6=sleep, 7=place_stone, 8=place_table, 9=place_furnace, 10=place_plant, 11=make_wood_pickaxe, 12=make_stone_pickaxe, 13=make_iron_pickaxe, 14=make_wood_sword, 15=make_stone_sword, 16=make_iron_sword. Eight keys are bound here, the rig's own (B and A beside the arrows, Y and X for the two menu buttons: the controller's, which a keyboard presses with the same letters). cycle and confirm have to be written as the literal ids 17 and 18: they are not crafter actions and nothing else names them. There is no '' entry, because turn_based means the loop steps only on a press. The ten menu actions are not listed anywhere: they are whatever the action space has left over, so a crafter that gained an action would put it in the menu rather than drop it. Keep the message Controls text in sync with 'keys' by hand.
_pacing_note: turn_based is true, which is the one place this parts company with the rig. Eight buttons cost more presses per action than seventeen keys, so a fixed cadence would spend the survival clock on menu cycling; here the world advances once per press and never otherwise, so the run is paced by the subject and every step is a decision. fps 15 is then a polling rate, not a game speed: it bounds how long a press waits to be seen (~67 ms), and it is what the other turn-based DBP configs use. latched_keys is irrelevant under turn_based -- the loop already reads keydowns -- and is left off. The rig has no turn-based mode at all: it runs a fixed 5 Hz cadence at half speed (frontend_pygame.py --cadence 5.0 --speed 0.5, i.e. 2.5 steps/s), so wall-clock comparisons with a rig run do not transfer and only the action sequences do.
_sleep_note: Sleep is the one place turn_based and stock crafter fight, and the fight is settled in the loop rather than in the rules, so the rules here are stock. Crafter takes no action from a sleeping player: Player.update overwrites it with sleep until energy is full (objects.py:99-131), and the step on which it fills is the one that wakes them and runs their action normally. Stock charges eleven sleeping steps per point of energy (_fatigue counts down and grants past -10), so three to a full nine is sixty-six steps: twenty-six seconds of a held key at 2.5 fps, but sixty-six presses of a button in a block where a step costs a press, and every one of those presses is thrown away by the engine. The adapter's autoplay returns noop while info['sleeping'] is set, and the loop steps at fps without waiting, so the sleep costs one press and about four seconds. Nothing about the game changes: the night still passes at its own rate, hunger, thirst and health still move at their sleeping rates, a zombie still closes in and still deals 7 to a sleeper against 2 awake (objects.py:305-308), and the frames are drawn and logged like any others, action noop, with a 'sleeping' column marking them. The wake is what the subject has to see and it is where the loop stops: a blow clears sleeping (_wake_up_when_hurt, objects.py:169-172), so the picture freezes on the frame with the zombie beside them and the health bar already down. Measured over 40 worlds asleep from step 150 (night, energy 0): a blow lands inside 66 steps in 32 of them, so this is a real decision and not a formality.
_hud_note: live_hud is true because a turn-based block draws a frame only when the subject presses, while the block still ends on the wall clock: without it the seconds in the HUD strip stop at the last press and a subject who is thinking sees a time that is not the time. It redraws the standing frame every 0.2 s through the wait and does nothing else -- no step, no log row, no trigger, no sound -- so the only thing it changes is the pixels. It is off by default and set only here; the other turn-based configs keep the behaviour they were run with.
_score_note: show_score draws the achievement count in the HUD strip above the frame, which crafter's own HUD does not show. It covers no game pixel and reports only values already in info['achievements'], so the model harness can be given the same scalar; if a model is ever evaluated without it, say so, because that is a difference in what the two players can see. The count is shown rather than the block's cumulative reward, which is the same quantity written less legibly: crafter pays +1 per first unlock and (health - last_health)/10 per step, and the health terms telescope to at most -0.9 over an episode.
_cue_note: cues turns on the three synthesized sounds in the adapter, because crafter itself ships none and three outcomes are otherwise invisible in the bore: a blow that landed on a creature without killing it (five bare-handed presses for a zombie), a press the engine refused (no pickaxe for that rock, no table in reach), and a press the rig dropped. score > hit > blocked, at most one a frame, since audio output queues rather than mixes. The cue is decided from the state the engine is about to act on, not by diffing state afterwards, which cannot see a non-lethal blow at all; it is exact because the player updates first every step, and it reads crafter's own collect/place/make tables without touching the world or its RNG. Collecting grass stays silent on purpose: data.yaml gives it probability 0.1, so a press that yields nothing is a failed roll, not a refusal. cue_overlay writes the same feedback as a field in the HUD strip, and it is off here deliberately: the subject has already heard the cue, so the field only repeats it, and a word appearing above the frame pulls the eyes off it between presses. The agent harness turns it on for itself, since a policy cannot hear a sound and would otherwise be told less than the subject was. The columns hit / no_effect / cue / target land in the npz however both flags are set.
_state_note: state_stride 25 counts frames, and a frame here is a press rather than a tick, so anchors fall every 25 presses. At size 384 a state is 2.3 MB and ~3 ms to write or read, but only 0.16 MB of that is the game: the rest is the observation space's constant bounds and the cached frame, and zlib leaves ~57 KB an anchor. A 300 s block played at 2.5 fps in real time (the pacing this config replaced, kept here because it is the measurement that exists) held 32 anchors, 76 MB raw and 1.8 MB compressed, and every one of them restored and then played its episode out frame-for-frame identically to the seed replay: that is what makes an anchor a branch point a model can be rolled out from. A turn-based block of the same duration has far fewer frames, so both the log and the anchor count shrink. The block's frames.h5 keeps the displayed pixels too (measured with per-frame zlib: 7.4 KB median in daylight; crafter mixes per-pixel noise into the view at night, so the 107 night frames of that block reached a median 185 KB and 217 KB at the worst, and the block came to 750 frames / 22.5 MB of pixels). Frames are kept even though the fork replays exactly, because they are the record that does not depend on whoever opens the block later having the fork installed. On stock crafter they are the only record: it rebalances creatures every tenth step by iterating a Python set of objects, so the despawn choice follows object id() and two runs of the same seed and actions diverge (measured 2026-09-28 across two PYTHONHASHSEEDs: step 30 of a 225-action episode, which then ended a step early; a restored anchor is worse off still, since unpickling renumbers every object). Terrain is identical either way; creatures are not.
_size_note: size 384 is an integer half of the 768-pixel display height, not the rig's GAME_PX 288. display.draw_frame scales unfiltered, so a fractional factor smears crafter's pixel art, and the counters crafter draws into the bottom two of its nine tile rows are what suffers first. Nothing about the game depends on it; crafter renders its 9x9 view at whatever size it is given. length 0 removes crafter's own 10000-step cap: the block is bounded by its duration, so every ending is a real death.

text: tools, eat, drink, sleep, and stay alive.
The world waits for you: it moves one step each
time you press a button, and not otherwise.
The menu holds the ten actions with no button of
their own: place stone, table, furnace, plant, and
make a wood / stone / iron pickaxe or sword. Y
moves the cursor and shows it over your character;
X performs it. Moving the cursor also costs a turn.
